name: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis

clinicalPearls: Thyrotoxicosis means a state of thyroid hormone excess and is not synonymous with hyperthyroidism, which specifically denotes excessive thyroid gland function; the major hyperthyroid causes are Graves' disease, toxic multinodular goiter, and toxic adenoma (Harrison 22e p.3032).

Graves' disease accounts for roughly 60-80% of thyrotoxicosis, occurs in up to 2% of women (about one-tenth as frequent in men), and typically presents between 20 and 50 years of age (Harrison 22e p.3032).

Graves' hyperthyroidism is driven by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins acting on the TSH receptor; TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) can be measured and, because they cross the placenta, are useful for monitoring pregnant Graves' patients for neonatal thyrotoxicosis (Harrison 22e p.3033).

Symptoms in descending frequency include hyperactivity/irritability, heat intolerance with sweating, palpitations, fatigue and weakness, weight loss with increased appetite, and diarrhea; signs include tachycardia (atrial fibrillation in the elderly), tremor, goiter, warm moist skin, and proximal myopathy (Harrison 22e p.3033).
Apathetic thyrotoxicosis in the elderly may present mainly with fatigue and weight loss and can be mistaken for depression; features may be subtle or masked in older patients (Harrison 22e p.3033).
Treating the thyrotoxic state alone converts atrial fibrillation to normal sinus rhythm in up to about 75% of patients without underlying cardiac disease (Harrison 22e p.3033).

Graves' ophthalmopathy (thyroid eye disease) is specific to Graves'; about one-third of patients have clinical eye disease, it can occur without hyperthyroidism in ~10%, and onset is within the year before or after thyrotoxicosis diagnosis in 75% (Harrison 22e p.3033).

Destructive (subacute or silent) thyroiditis causes a transient thyrotoxic phase from release of preformed hormone with characteristically LOW radionuclide uptake and elevated thyroglobulin; true hyperthyroidism is absent (Harrison 22e p.3035).

Subacute (de Quervain's) thyroiditis classically evolves through three phases over about 6 months: thyrotoxic, then hypothyroid, then recovery; it is supported by a high ESR and a tender goiter, and the T4/T3 ratio is higher (T3 less disproportionately elevated) than in Graves' or thyroid autonomy (Harrison 22e p.3038).

Toxic multinodular goiter typically affects elderly patients with subclinical or mild overt hyperthyroidism, often presenting with atrial fibrillation; iodine exposure (e.g., contrast dye) can precipitate thyrotoxicosis, and the scan shows heterogeneous patchy uptake (Harrison 22e p.3042).

A toxic (hyperfunctioning) adenoma usually causes only mild thyrotoxicosis, generally detectable when the nodule exceeds about 3 cm, and over 90% harbor activating somatic mutations in the TSH receptor or GSalpha (Harrison 22e p.3043).

Mild hypercalcemia occurs in up to 20% of thyrotoxic patients (hypercalciuria is more common), and longstanding thyrotoxicosis causes osteopenia with a small increase in fracture rate due to direct stimulation of bone resorption (Harrison 22e p.3033).
harrison.pathophysiology: Graves' disease results from a combination of genetic susceptibility (HLA-DR and immunoregulatory genes such as CTLA-4, CD25, CD40, PTPN22, plus the TSH-R gene) and environmental triggers (smoking, stress, sudden iodine excess, the postpartum period, and immune reconstitution after HAART, alemtuzumab, or immune checkpoint inhibitors). Hyperthyroidism is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins that bind and stimulate the TSH receptor; coexisting lymphocytic thyroiditis (TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies in up to 80%) means there is no direct correlation between TSI level and hormone levels. Ophthalmopathy reflects activated T-cell infiltration of extraocular muscles with cytokine-driven (IFN-gamma, TNF, IL-1) fibroblast activation, glycosaminoglycan accumulation that traps water and causes muscle swelling, increased orbital fat, and late irreversible fibrosis; the TSH-R is an orbital autoantigen and aberrant IGF-1 receptor signaling on orbital fibroblasts contributes. In destructive thyroiditis, follicular disruption releases preformed hormone (low radionuclide uptake). Toxic multinodular goiter reflects acquired functional autonomy of nodules, while toxic adenoma reflects constitutive cyclic AMP signaling from activating TSH-R or GSalpha mutations.
additionalDifferentials: Graves' disease (diffuse goiter, ophthalmopathy, positive TRAb, high diffuse radionuclide uptake)
Toxic adenoma (focal hot nodule, suppressed surrounding uptake)
Subacute (de Quervain's) thyroiditis (painful tender goiter, high ESR, low uptake)
Silent/postpartum thyroiditis (painless, low uptake, TPO antibodies, normal ESR)
Thyrotoxicosis factitia (exogenous hormone; low thyroglobulin, low uptake)
TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma (non-suppressed TSH with high T4)
Struma ovarii and functioning metastatic follicular carcinoma (ectopic thyroid tissue)
infectionMimics: Subacute viral thyroiditis from mumps, coxsackie, influenza, adenovirus, echovirus, or SARS-CoV-2, which can mimic pharyngitis with sore throat and fever during the thyrotoxic phase (Harrison 22e p.3038)
nonInfectiousMimics: Depression (especially apathetic thyrotoxicosis in the elderly)
additionalInvestigations: Serum TSH (suppressed) with unbound (free) T4 and T3; isolated T3 elevation indicates T3 toxicosis (2-5%), and isolated T4 elevation can occur with iodine-induced disease
TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) to confirm Graves' when classic features are absent

Radionuclide (99mTc, 123I, or 131I) thyroid scan and uptake to distinguish high diffuse uptake of Graves' from low uptake of destructive thyroiditis, factitious thyrotoxicosis, and to identify toxic adenoma or toxic MNG
Color-flow Doppler ultrasonography (increased flow in hyperthyroidism vs destructive thyroiditis) when avoiding radioactivity
ESR (elevated in subacute thyroiditis, normal in silent thyroiditis) and thyroglobulin (low in factitia)

Orbital CT or MRI and ophthalmologic assessment (lid-fissure width, corneal fluorescein staining, extraocular muscle/Hess chart, intraocular pressure, visual fields, acuity, color vision) for ophthalmopathy
Pituitary CT/MRI when TSH is non-suppressed with elevated T4 (suspected TSH-secreting adenoma)
Fine-needle aspiration of cold nodules in toxic MNG when sonographic features warrant
redFlags: Thyrotoxic crisis (thyroid storm): fever, delirium, seizures, coma, vomiting, diarrhea, and jaundice with a high mortality (about 4-17% even with treatment)
New or worsening atrial fibrillation or high-output heart failure, particularly in the elderly or those with preexisting cardiac disease
Sight-threatening ophthalmopathy from optic nerve compression (papilledema, peripheral field defects, loss of vision) or corneal ulceration/exposure
Thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis (notably in Asian males)
Diplopia or severe proptosis with corneal exposure during sleep
harrison.prognosis: Untreated, clinical features generally worsen and mortality was historically 10-30% before effective therapy. Some patients with mild Graves' disease have spontaneous relapses and remissions, and about 15% of those who enter remission develop hypothyroidism 10-15 years later from ongoing autoimmune destruction. Ophthalmopathy follows an independent course, typically worsening over 3-6 months, plateauing over the next 12-18 months, then partially improving, though up to ~5% have a fulminant course. Subacute thyroiditis usually resolves completely, with late permanent hypothyroidism in about 15%. Thyrotoxic crisis carries a high mortality (about 4-17%) even with treatment, due to cardiac failure, arrhythmia, or hyperthermia. Toxic multinodular goiter and toxic adenoma do not remit spontaneously and require definitive therapy.
pitfalls: Equating thyrotoxicosis with hyperthyroidism: destructive thyroiditis, factitia, and iodine excess cause hormone excess without true gland hyperfunction (low uptake)
Missing apathetic thyrotoxicosis in the elderly, where it can present as fatigue/weight loss or be mistaken for depression or malignancy
Overlooking that there is no direct correlation between TSI level and hormone levels because coexisting thyroiditis affects function

Interpreting thyroid function tests during acute severe illness (sick euthyroid/nonthyroidal illness) as true thyroid disease; routine testing in acutely ill patients should be avoided, though an undetectable TSH (<0.01 mIU/L) makes primary thyroid disease more likely
Failing to recognize that radioiodine therapy can worsen ophthalmopathy in a small proportion of patients, especially smokers
Attributing clubbing to thyroid acropachy in a Graves' patient who lacks coincident dermopathy and ophthalmopathy, where another cause should be sought
harrison.severityClassification: Graves' ophthalmopathy is graded by the NO SPECS mnemonic (0 no signs/symptoms; 1 only signs such as lid retraction/lag; 2 soft tissue involvement/periorbital edema; 3 proptosis >22 mm; 4 extraocular muscle involvement/diplopia; 5 corneal involvement; 6 sight loss), although activity-based systems such as EUGOGO are preferred for monitoring and treatment decisions. Thyrotoxicosis itself ranges from subclinical (low TSH, normal free T4/T3) to overt disease and may escalate to thyrotoxic crisis/thyroid storm.
management: Thionamide antithyroid drugs such as carbimazole or propylthiouracil to control Graves' disease and toxic nodular hyperthyroidism
Definitive therapy with radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy for relapsing or nodular disease, with thyroxine replacement thereafter
Beta-blockade to relieve adrenergic symptoms and control tachyarrhythmia, with anticoagulation considered for thyrotoxic atrial fibrillation
Manage destructive thyroiditis supportively without antithyroid drugs, using beta-blockers and anti-inflammatory agents for subacute thyroiditis
Treat thyroid storm as an emergency with thionamide, iodine, beta-blocker, corticosteroids and supportive care
Manage Graves' ophthalmopathy with smoking cessation, selenium, corticosteroids, orbital radiotherapy or decompression, and teprotumumab in active disease
In pregnancy prefer propylthiouracil in the first trimester and monitor TSH receptor antibodies for neonatal thyrotoxicosis
Monitor thyroid function during and after treatment, anticipating later hypothyroidism
